- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., < 0.33) and supply net is large negative, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overshoots and fails to adjust — apply downward drag or lagged smoothing to prevent overreaction.
- In high-event periods (e.g., >15 events/30d, net supply negative), model underestimates downside risk — increase downward bias or add volatility penalty to forecast.
- When bullish sentiment is low but supply is negative, model often ignores bearish pressure — adjust forecast downward by 5–10% of recent mean if sentiment < 0.67.
- Model tends to ignore sentiment shifts in early days of event window — if sentiment flips from bullish to bearish within 3 days, adjust forecast downward by 2–5% per day.
- In multi-event weeks (e.g., 20+ auctions), model overfits to recent price trends — apply exponential decay to recent forecast weights or use 18-day moving average for smoothing.
- If true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days below 60), model often fails to recognize — add mean-reversion term to forecast, e.g., target 60–65 as baseline.
- When sentiment is neutral or mixed (0.33–0.67) and supply is negative, model often underestimates risk — add 3–5% downward buffer to forecast if supply net < -10.
- In high-bearish sentiment (e.g., >0.67 bearish) with low bullish, model often fails to adjust — apply downward bias of 2–5% per day if sentiment > 0.67 and supply net < -10.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows sharp drop, model is lagging — apply 1–2 day lag correction or add 5–10% downward adjustment if true outcome drops >10% from prior day.
